packageText: TITLE: Varicocele CANONICAL ROUTING - Canonical hierarchy: All Categories > Basic > Ultrasound > Scrotum Basic > Varicocele - Canonical deck path: Corebook::Ultrasound::Scrotum Basic::Varicocele - Hierarchy source: metadata.json canonicalHierarchy copied from RadPrimer breadcrumbTrail. - IMAIOS/package routing: derive any breadcrumb, deckPath, or tags from the canonical hierarchy above; do not substitute STATdx breadcrumbs. SOURCE BASIS - [RadPrimer] Canonical article backbone and hierarchy. - [STATdx] Supplemental diagnostic depth, image variants, complications, differential detail, and treatment nuance. - No auditable Core Radiology passage was present in the supplied bundle, so no Core-specific claims are added. IMAGE COVERAGE GATE - Actual downloaded image_evidence files were inspected before duplicate classification. - No RadPrimer image is a proven exact duplicate of a STATdx image. There are no matching stable source image IDs, no matching image hashes, and no visually identical same-slice/same-screenshot pairs in the evidence set. - STATdx conceptually covers the RadPrimer image set, but the overlap is useful reinforcement rather than duplicate waste. - RadPrimer image 1: conceptual replacement by STATdx image 4; both retained because the graphics are visually different and complementary. - RadPrimer image 2: near duplicate/conceptual overlap with STATdx grayscale examples, especially STATdx images 1, 14, 15, and 17; all retained because views and cases differ. - RadPrimer image 3: near duplicate/conceptual overlap with STATdx Doppler/Valsalva examples, especially STATdx images 2, 3, 10, 11, 16, and 18; all retained as distinct Doppler recognition examples. - RadPrimer image 4: conceptual replacement/procedure complement by STATdx image 12; both retained because RadPrimer shows a prominent gonadal vein/varicocele venogram context and STATdx shows post-coil lack of reflux. - Archive decision: no images archived by default; all 22 source images remain in the primary teaching set. MASTER IMAGE SET - Primary teaching images: all RadPrimer images 1-4 and all STATdx images 1-18. - Archive optional images: none. - Preserve source case clusters: STATdx images 1-2, 7-9, 10-12, and 14-16. KEY FACTS - [Both] Varicocele is dilation and tortuosity of veins of the pampiniform plexus, classically greater than 3 mm, caused by venous congestion and retrograde flow in the internal spermatic/testicular vein. - [Both] Best imaging clue: dilated, serpiginous/tubular veins adjacent to or behind the superior pole of the testis, with increased color Doppler flow or reflux during Valsalva. - [RadPrimer] Distribution: left sided is most common, right sided is uncommon, and bilateral disease is less common than isolated left-sided disease. - [STATdx] Isolated right-sided varicocele is uncommon but is rarely associated with malignancy when no other concerning symptoms are present; retroperitoneal imaging may be unnecessary in otherwise reassuring adult cases, though US retroperitoneal assessment can be considered during the same exam. - [Both] Valsalva is essential for small varicoceles; exam should include rest and Valsalva color Doppler. - [STATdx] ESUR-style protocol: evaluate with and without Valsalva, supine and standing; measure the largest vein regardless of location; 3 mm or greater is diagnostic; report testicular volume when relevant. - [Both] Varicocele is a frequent/treatable cause of male infertility, but many patients have normal semen parameters. TERMINOLOGY - [Both] Definition: dilation of pampiniform plexus veins greater than 3 mm due to retrograde flow in the testicular/internal spermatic vein. - [STATdx] Dilated veins may involve the pampiniform plexus, cremasteric plexus, vein of vas deferens, and testicular/spermatic vein. - [Both] Intratesticular varicocele is rare and involves dilated veins at the mediastinum testis; it must be distinguished from tubular ectasia of the rete testis. IMAGING - [Both] Ultrasound with color Doppler is the best diagnostic tool. Use high-frequency scrotal US with supine and standing assessment when possible. - [Both] Grayscale US shows hypoechoic, tubular, serpiginous vessels superior/posterior/lateral to the testis; they may extend along the spermatic cord. - [Both] Diagnostic size threshold: multiple pampiniform plexus veins greater than or equal to 3 mm, especially upright or during Valsalva. - [Both] Color Doppler shows distention and increased flow/reflux with Valsalva. Slow flow can be missed unless low Doppler settings are used. - [STATdx] If the Doppler scale is set appropriately, retrograde flow is directed toward the testis; reflux longer than 2 seconds during Valsalva is diagnostic of significant reflux. - [STATdx] Slow venous flow can appear echogenic and mobile in real time and should not be mistaken for thrombus; true thrombosis is echogenic material in a noncompressible lumen without flow during Valsalva. - [RadPrimer] MRI is usually incidental and shows serpiginous enhancing channels; slow flow can be intermediate T1 and high T2 signal, while higher velocity flow may create signal voids. - [Both] Catheter venography demonstrates dilated venous channels and can document gonadal/testicular vein reflux; treatment may be catheter embolization. - [STATdx] CT or MR may show enhancing tubular structures or reveal secondary venous causes such as renal vein thrombosis, retroperitoneal tumor, fibrosis, or systemic venous congestion. - [RadPrimer] Scan the retroperitoneum for mass when clinical context suggests a secondary cause, especially recent-onset varicocele in an older patient. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS - [STATdx] Hernia: echogenic fat or bowel displaces the testis, may accentuate with Valsalva, shows gut signature/peristalsis, and has minimal bowel-content Doppler flow. - [Both] Epididymitis: enlarged heterogeneous epididymis with increased Doppler flow, separate from the pampiniform plexus, and without Valsalva-dependent varicocele reflux behavior. - [Both] Tubular ectasia of the rete testis: avascular dilated tubules in the mediastinum testis; no Doppler flow, unlike intratesticular varicocele. - [STATdx] Spermatocele/epididymal cyst: one or more anechoic or hypoechoic cysts without Doppler flow. - [STATdx] Rare vascular lesions: testicular AVM, hemangioma, or high-flow extratesticular mass. - [RadPrimer] Testicular torsion: enlarged hypoechoic testis with absent or decreased intratesticular flow. PATHOLOGY AND MECHANISM - [Both] Primary varicocele is related to venous valve incompetence and reflux, classically near the left renal vein/IVC junction. - [Both] Left-sided predominance is explained by the longer left testicular vein and its perpendicular drainage into the left renal vein; the right testicular vein drains more directly into the IVC. - [Both] Secondary causes include obstruction or compression of testicular venous drainage by renal/adrenal tumor, retroperitoneal nodes, lymphoma, RCC, retroperitoneal fibrosis, renal vein thrombosis, or nutcracker-type SMA compression. - [Both] Potential fertility injury mechanisms include increased scrotal/testicular heat, oxidative stress, stagnant blood/ischemia, increased venous pressure with decreased arterial inflow, catecholamine reflux, and androgen deprivation. - [RadPrimer] Clinical grading: small is palpable only with Valsalva, moderate is palpable with standing, and large is visible through scrotal skin and palpable while standing. CLINICAL ISSUES - [Both] Many varicoceles are asymptomatic and detected on physical exam or infertility work-up. - [Both] Typical symptoms are vague scrotal discomfort, pressure, or heaviness, usually worse while standing. - [Both] Varicocele is common in the general male population and more common among infertile men, but many men with varicocele have normal fertility and normal semen parameters. - [STATdx] In adults, repair is generally considered for men trying to conceive who have palpable varicocele and abnormal semen parameters, or for scrotal pain. - [STATdx] There is no indication to treat subclinical varicoceles found only by imaging; men with azoospermia may not benefit. Adolescent treatment is controversial and may use testicular volume discrepancy. - [Both] Treatment options include catheter embolization/sclerotherapy and surgical ligation. STATdx notes that varicocelectomy is a misnomer because veins are ligated rather than removed. DIAGNOSTIC CHECKLIST - [Both] Perform Valsalva; small varicoceles may be occult without it. - [Both] Confirm venous structure, diameter, and reflux rather than relying on gray-scale serpiginous appearance alone. - [STATdx] Use Doppler settings sensitive enough for slow flow and reflux; avoid mistaking very slow flow for thrombosis. - [RadPrimer] In an older man with new-onset varicocele, consider left renal vein occlusion or retroperitoneal/renal/adrenal tumor. - [STATdx] In adults with isolated right-sided varicocele and no other malignancy symptoms, recent experience does not support frequent cancer association; in children younger than 9 years, look for tumor. - [Both] Measure/report testicular volume when fertility or adolescent testicular function is part of the question. IMAGE CATALOG FOR FUTURE GENERATION - RadPrimer image 1: Graphic shows dilated, tortuous varicose veins of the pampiniform plexus in the spermatic cord and along the posterosuperior aspect of the testis . - RadPrimer image 2: Oblique grayscale ultrasound through the cord, in supine position with normal respiration, shows a dilated, tortuous principal vein in the pampiniform plexus measuring 7.5 mm in caliber. - RadPrimer image 3: Longitudinal color Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum in a 24-year-old man shows flow in several dilated veins during Valsalva, indicative of moderate varicocele. Blood flow in the varicocele is slow and may be detected only with low Doppler settings. - RadPrimer image 4: Catheter venogram demonstrates a prominent left gonadal vein extending into the left hemiscrotum in this patient with varicocele and infertility. Varicocele resolved after coil embolization. - STATdx image 1: Transverse US of the left scrotum with the patient at rest in supine position shows multiple anechoic, tubular structures medial to the testis, consistent with varicocele. - STATdx image 2: Longitudinal color Doppler US in the same patient during Valsalva shows flow throughout the varicocele due to reflux. - STATdx image 3: Longitudinal color Doppler US shows dilated veins with minimal flow at rest . With Valsalva , aliasing is seen due to increased velocity of retrograde blood flow exceeding the low Doppler scale. - STATdx image 4: Graphic shows normal pampiniform plexus veins compared to abnormally dilated veins in a varicocele . - STATdx image 5: Transverse US inferior to the testis shows a large, right-sided varicocele . Some of the veins are echogenic due to slow flow (mobile in real time). The patient underwent CT, which was negative. Right-sided varicoceles, without other symptoms of malignancy, are rarely associated with an underlying malignancy. - STATdx image 6: Longitudinal US of the spermatic cord just superior to the testis in a patient with palpable, painful area shows a thrombosed varicocele vein as a echogenic, expanded vein without color flow. - STATdx image 7: Coronal CECT in a patient with history of severe necrotizing pancreatitis shows large, dilated veins in the left hemiscrotum , consistent with varicocele. These communicate with the spermatic (gonadal) vein . - STATdx image 8: Coronal CECT in the same patient shows a dilated spermatic vein entering a small left renal vein . - STATdx image 9: Axial CECT in the same patient shows chronic thrombosis of the left renal vein due to past pancreatitis. Rarely, secondary causes of varicocele include vascular thromboses, iatrogenic causes, and tumor compression/venous invasion. - STATdx image 10: Longitudinal color Doppler US of the left scrotum in a 20-year-old symptomatic patient shows dilated vessels with scattered Doppler signal at rest. - STATdx image 11: Longitudinal color Doppler US in the same patient with Valsalva shows increased size of vessels and marked increase in flow due to retrograde flow in the pampiniform plexus. - STATdx image 12: Anterior projection venogram in the same patient after coil embolization of the varicocele shows lack of reflux caudal to the coil mass . - STATdx image 13: Transverse color Doppler US shows tortuous, hypoechoic structures in the testis at the mediastinum with minimal flow. Rarely, a varicocele extends into or occurs primarily in the testis. This should not be confused with dilation of the rete testis. - STATdx image 14: Transverse US of both testes shows multiple hypoechoic, tubular structures along the medial aspect of the left testis. - STATdx image 15: Longitudinal US of the left scrotum in the same patient shows the tubular and serpiginous nature of the lesion . - STATdx image 16: Color Doppler US in the same patient with Valsalva shows marked blood flow , consistent with a moderate-sized varicocele. - STATdx image 17: Longitudinal US of the right scrotum in the setting of a palpable mass shows an isolated, right-sided varicocele . Further work-up showed no malignancy. In the past, this was thought to be highly associated with malignancy; however, more recent experience shows that isolated, right-sided varicocele is rarely associated with malignancy. When it does occur in the setting of malignancy, there are often other concerning symptoms. - STATdx image 18: Color Doppler US in an older man with scrotal discomfort shows a huge left varicocele. The late onset prompted imaging of the retroperitoneum, which showed marked dilatation of the cava and renal veins due to severe right heart dysfunction. TRACEABILITY NOTES - Human-facing prose should use labels such as RadPrimer image 2 or STATdx image 11. - Registry IDs and source-qualified filenames retain RP-/SDX-style traceability codes for import, download, and audit fields. - The selectedPrimaryImageIds and sourceSelectionPlan.imageDownloadPlan fields in the JSON outputs define the curated image download set.
